highlights: Self-driving two-wheeled telepresence robot for remote work and education
Click-to-Drive uses 3D sensing and overlays to guide remote navigation
Two cameras provide an adjustable pan, tilt and zoom view

The Double 3 FAQ gives approximately 7.3 kg (16 lb), up to four hours of normal-use runtime and about two hours for a full recharge. Remotely adjustable height is 47–60 inches, roughly 120–150 cm in the FAQ; this is a height range rather than complete length/width/height.

The integrated head combines two 13 MP cameras, six beamforming microphones, two RealSense D430 depth modules, five ultrasonic range finders and Jetson TX2-4GB compute. The listed nine-DoF IMU describes inertial sensing, not nine independently actuated robot joints.

Click-to-Drive accepts a driver-selected visible floor target and handles local obstacle avoidance. SDK documentation also describes clicking a charging-dock icon. Full-building automatic mapping and path planning remain future features on the overview page; collision-free operation is not independently guaranteed.

Double 3 uses Wi-Fi for Internet access according to the FAQ. Bluetooth 4.2 hardware does not establish native cellular service; the iPhone-mediated LTE/4G control described for the camera-dolly configuration is a different scope.

The manufacturer offers a Double 3 head upgrade for existing Double 2 bases. That head and the five trim colors are accessories/configuration choices, not additional complete robot generations. The developer page describes ROS connectors as a future possibility, not installed ROS support.

In their September 10, 2019 interview, the co-founders described Double 3 orders at 3999 USD with first shipments planned for late September. That historical announcement does not establish today’s price or actual shipment dates; the current homepage says Sold Out. The unsupported previous 1.0 m/s speed and generic medium size label are omitted.

Public SDK documents describe Ubuntu 18.04/aarch64 applications and power/performance modes; higher compute workloads can change power use. Published software history is not proof that accounts, cloud calling, updates or support remain available today. Professional Fleet Management is a separate software plan, not a hardware purchase price.

highlights: Lateral stability control is described as a shock-absorption mechanism for ordinary office/classroom floor obstructions. Power Drive is claimed to be up to 80 percent faster than normal driving; no exact absolute speed or general obstacle-climbing rating is established here.

The optional Camera Kit provides a five-megapixel, 150-degree wide-angle camera, always-on floor view and Adaptive HD. It uses the iPad Lightning connector and passes charging power through; camera-kit capability is not silently assigned to every bare Double 2.

The manufacturer states that Camera Kit also works with first-generation Double and that first-generation Charging Dock and Audio Kit accessories work with Double 2. Its Double 3 head upgrade fits Double 2 bases. Accessories and retrofits do not create a second duplicate identity for the same base.

The retained iPad-era Revision 13 manual explains Bluetooth pairing, keyboard driving and roughly two-to-three-hour charging, but is not explicitly generation-titled. Its generic values and Double 3’s newer four-hour runtime are not imported as exact Double 2 battery specifications. Current availability and an exact initial launch year remain unverified in the selected primary material.

Double Robotics — Double 2 and optional Camera Kit

highlights: The named package contains a Double 2 base, Universal 360 Camera Mount and customized Pelican travel case. The page lists 3000 USD for the package and 249 USD for the mount alone, without a publication date or verified current checkout. Neither the bare mount nor travel case is an extra robot model.

The manufacturer limits attachment weight at the top to five pounds, approximately 2.27 kg, and allows an unspecified few additional pounds near the base. This is a top-mount configuration limit, not a measured total chassis payload, lifting capacity or a load rating for other Double generations.

The aluminum mount uses a quarter-inch, twenty-thread attachment and holds an iPhone for driving from behind the scenes. The FAQ names an iPhone 6 or earlier, or iPod touch, for remote driving. This historical compatibility statement does not establish current apps, cellular service or operating-system support.

The six-GoPro rig and stitched sample footage illustrate an external camera setup; the package inclusion list names no camera. Quiet-operation marketing has no published decibel test here. The platform is remotely operated, without a claim of autonomous cinematography, obstacle avoidance or current support continuity.

companyFocus.name: Double Robotics
companyFocus.role: Mobile telepresence robots and a named Double 2 camera-dolly configuration; fleet software and developer tools
highlights: Original Double, iPad-based Double 2 and integrated-head Double 3 are distinct generations. The named 360 Camera Dolly packages a Double 2 base with a camera mount and case. Head upgrades, Camera Kit, Charging Dock, Audio Kit, camera mounts and trim colors remain accessories or choices, not additional complete robots.

The issuer confirms original Double shipments began May 2013. Named founders discuss Double 3 orders and planned late-September shipping in a September 2019 interview. The current homepage says Sold Out; retained pages do not prove worldwide stock, company closure, universal discontinuation or continued calling/support service.

Double 3 offers user-selected Click-to-Drive with local obstacle assistance; full-building mapping/path planning is still described as future functionality. The developer page describes possible future ROS connectors. Neither statement is presented as verified installed capability on every device.

Public Fleet Management information distinguishes a free Basic tier from Professional at 79.20 USD per robot per month billed yearly or 99 USD monthly. These displayed software prices are separate from hardware prices and do not establish current subscription checkout availability. Listed SSO, calendar reservations and call-quality logs remain vendor-described functions.

The public D3 SDK documents custom applications and sensor access. Fleet REST documentation and API keys require an account; no account or device endpoint was accessed. The earlier blog redirects to a private password page and two support pages fail. Historical browser requirements, encryption statements and release history do not establish current security compliance, service continuity or performance guarantees.
